examples: I have a meeting in the morning.
I am usually busy in the morning.
nuance: 오전 means the AM period before noon and is more formal than 아침. Use it with clock times like 오전 9시.
mistakes: Saying 오전 시간 when you just mean 아침 (early morning)

examples: I meet a friend in the afternoon.
I have an appointment at 2 PM.
nuance: 오후 covers all PM hours from noon until evening. With clock times, say the period first: 오후 5시, not 5시 오후.
mistakes: Putting 오후 after the time, like 다섯 시 오후

examples: I drink coffee in the morning.
nuance: 아침 means both early morning and the breakfast meal. Context tells them apart: 아침에 is the time, 아침을 먹다 is the meal.
mistakes: Using 오전 for the breakfast meal instead of 아침

examples: What do you eat for lunch?
nuance: 점심 means both the midday time and the lunch meal. Koreans often greet with 점심 먹었어요? meaning have you eaten lunch.
mistakes: Confusing 점심 (lunch) with 정심, a misspelling

examples: I watch a movie in the evening.
nuance: 저녁 means both the early-night period and the dinner meal. It comes after 오후 but before 밤 (late night).
mistakes: Using 밤 for the dinner meal instead of 저녁

examples: I do not sleep well at night.
nuance: 밤 is late night, later than 저녁. 어제 밤 means last night, while 내일 밤 means tomorrow night.
mistakes: Using 저녁 when you mean late night 밤

examples: I go to school on Monday.
nuance: 요일 is the suffix for weekday names: 월요일, 화요일, and so on. To ask the day, say 무슨 요일이에요, not 어떤 요일.
mistakes: Asking 어느 요일이에요 instead of the natural 무슨 요일이에요

examples: I usually rest on the weekend.
What are you doing this weekend?
nuance: 주말 covers Saturday and Sunday. A common Friday farewell is 주말 잘 보내세요, meaning have a good weekend.
mistakes: Saying 주말에서 instead of 주말에 for the time when something happens

nuance: 어제 is a time word that usually drops the particle 에. It naturally pairs with past-tense verbs ending in 았어요 or 었어요.
mistakes: Adding 에 like 어제에; time words 어제 오늘 내일 usually drop it

examples: Please give me one of these.
nuance: 개 counts general objects and uses native Korean numbers, which change shape: 하나 becomes 한, 둘 becomes 두 before 개.
mistakes: Using Sino numbers like 일 개; use native 한 개, 두 개

nuance: 명 counts people and uses native numbers like 한 명, 두 명. The polite counter 분 replaces 명 when honoring guests or elders.
mistakes: Using 개 for people instead of 명

examples: How much is this? It is 3000 won.
nuance: 원 is the Korean currency and always takes Sino-Korean numbers: 천 원, 만 원. Note 만 원 means 10000 won, not 1000.
mistakes: Using native numbers like 한 원; prices use Sino 천, 만
